DeGMatch: Target-Aware Reasoning Data Selection via Deconfounded Gradient Matching

Changho Lee Affiliation: University of Michigan Email: changhol@umich.edu    Janghoon Han Affiliation: University of Texas at Dallas    Rajdeep Mukherjee Affiliation: University of Michigan    Yeda Song Affiliation: University of Michigan    Lening Nick Cui Affiliation: University of Michigan    Xinya Du Affiliation: University of Texas at Dallas    Honglak Lee Affiliation: University of Michigan Affiliation: LG AI Research
Abstract

Reasoning post-training on long trajectories has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but scaling such training to large datasets is increasingly expensive. We study target-aware reasoning data selection, where a small reference set specifies a target capability and guides the selection of training trajectories for specialization. We find that existing target-aware methods can exhibit limited target discrimination on long reasoning trajectories, while dominant population-level structure in candidate gradients can obscure finer target-dependent variation during gradient matching. To address these limitations, we introduce Deconfounded Gradient Matching (DeGMatch), which first constructs a target-relevance gate and then reranks candidates using model-specific gradients. DeGMatch centers gradients using the candidate-population mean and removes leading principal directions before target matching, reducing the influence of dominant population-level structure and improving target discrimination. Across mathematics, science, and code, DeGMatch outperforms strong heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific data selection baselines, while remaining effective across selection budgets, model families, and scales. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CHLee0801/degmatch.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in large language models have yielded substantial improvements in complex reasoning capabilities (DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Yang et al., 2025). Reasoning post-training has emerged as a standard approach to enhancing these capabilities through training on long reasoning trajectories (Guha et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025a; Yuan et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025a). However, the growing scale of reasoning datasets and the length of individual trajectories make full-data training increasingly computationally expensive. This has motivated growing interest in data-efficient reasoning post-training, where carefully selected subsets of reasoning trajectories can achieve competitive performance with substantially less training data (Yang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026d; Yu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a).

While data-efficient selection seeks compact subsets that are broadly useful for post-training, many real-world applications require specialization to a particular downstream task or capability rather than broad, general-purpose competence (Xia et al., 2024). For such specialization, training examples that benefit general reasoning performance may not be those that best support the target capability. This motivates target-aware data selection, which aims to identify training examples that most effectively support a specified downstream objective. Prior work has explored this paradigm in instruction tuning and general data-selection settings, using target similarity or distribution matching to identify target-relevant examples, and gradient-based signals to estimate their training utility for a specified target (Liu et al., 2024b; Ivison et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025; Min et al., 2026).

However, applying gradient-based matching to long reasoning trajectories reveals an important limitation. We find that candidate gradients are dominated by a small number of population-level directions: across five mathematical target-conditioned candidate populations, the top 50 principal components explain 86.7–89.4% of the centered-gradient variance. The leading principal subspaces also remain substantially aligned across candidate populations induced by different targets. As shown in Figure 1, rankings formed from the dominant subspace exhibit limited fine-grained target separation, whereas removing these dominant directions yields more distinguishable target-dependent ranking structure. These results suggest that dominant population-level gradient structure can obscure finer target-dependent variation during gradient matching.

Motivated by this analysis, we introduce DeGMatch, which suppresses dominant population-level structure in candidate gradients to better expose target-dependent variation during gradient matching. DeGMatch first restricts selection to a target-relevant candidate region. Within this region, it computes gradients with respect to the model being post-trained and, inspired by common-component removal in representation learning (Mu et al., 2018), centers gradients using the candidate-population mean and removes the leading principal directions estimated from the candidate gradients before target matching. DeGMatch then scores candidates using directional alignment with target gradients together with their gradient magnitude in the target-gradient subspace.

Empirically, DeGMatch consistently outperforms strong heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific data selection baselines across multiple reasoning domains. On mathematical reasoning, it achieves the strongest aggregate performance among selection methods and the best result on six of eight benchmarks, while also outperforming competing selection methods on scientific reasoning and code generation. Further analyses show that DeGMatch remains effective across different deconfounding settings and selection budgets, as well as across model families and scales.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We identify limited target discrimination in target-aware selection on long reasoning trajectories and show that, for gradient-based matching, dominant population-level structure in candidate gradients can obscure finer target-dependent variation.

  • •

    We introduce DeGMatch, which combines target-relevant retrieval with deconfounded, model-specific gradient matching for efficient reasoning specialization.

  • •

    We show that DeGMatch outperforms strong heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific baselines across reasoning domains, and remains effective across deconfounding settings and selection budgets, as well as across model families and scales.

2 Related Work

2.1 Target-Aware Data Selection

Target-aware data selection builds on broader data-selection literature, which uses signals such as quality, complexity, or diversity (Chen et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a), likelihood or learnability (Mindermann et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024a), semantic representations (Chen et al., 2025b), and model-dependent utility (Agarwal et al., 2025). Target-aware approaches further condition selection on a downstream task or reference set through distribution matching (Xie et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024b), target similarity (Ivison et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2024), or optimization-based signals (Xia et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025b; Min et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026c). These methods have primarily been studied in instruction-tuning or general data-selection settings, whereas we investigate their transfer to long reasoning trajectories and address limited target discrimination in gradient matching.

2.2 Reasoning-Specific Data Selection

Reasoning-data curation has explored problem difficulty and trajectory structure (Yang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025), step-level likelihood or uncertainty (Just et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), and length confounding in likelihood-based selection (Wang et al., 2026). Student-dependent signals include rank–surprisal, token entropy, perturbation-based loss dynamics, learnability, skill coverage, and capability–difficulty alignment (Yang et al., 2026d; Li et al., 2026c; Jin et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026a). Other work adapts the generation or selection of teacher supervision to the student (He et al., 2026; Yun et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a) or uses gradient-related signals for curation and reinforcement learning (Li et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026b). Unlike these approaches, which generally emphasize reasoning-data quality or student suitability, we condition selection on an explicit target capability specified by a small reference set.

2.3 Gradient-Based Data Selection and Geometry

Gradient information has been widely used for influence estimation (Koh and Liang, 2017; Pruthi et al., 2020; Kwon et al., 2024), subset and coreset selection (Mirzasoleiman et al., 2020; Killamsetty et al., 2021b; Killamsetty et al., 2021a; Paul et al., 2021), and target-conditioned data selection (Xia et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025b; Min et al., 2026). Prior work also shows that gradient representations can exhibit substantial covariance, low-rank, and spectral structure (Achille et al., 2019; Rame et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2026), and that normalization or whitening can substantially change their similarity geometry (Ma et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025). Common-component removal has similarly been used to suppress dominant shared directions in representation spaces (Mu et al., 2018). Building on these geometric perspectives, we suppress dominant candidate-population directions before target matching to improve discrimination across targets.

3 DeGMatch

DeGMatch selects reasoning trajectories in three stages: it first restricts the candidate pool to target-relevant examples, then removes dominant candidate-population structure from the gradient geometry, and finally ranks candidates through target-conditioned gradient matching. Figure 2 illustrates the overall procedure.

3.1 Problem Formulation

Let 𝒟pool={zi}i=1N\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pool}}=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote a large pool of reasoning trajectories, where zi=(xi,yi)z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i}) consists of a problem xix_{i} and its reasoning trajectory yiy_{i}. Let 𝒟target={aj}j=1M\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{target}}=\{a_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M} be a small reference set specifying a target capability, with aj=(xjt,yjt)a_{j}=(x_{j}^{t},y_{j}^{t}). Given a model with parameters θ0\theta_{0} and a selection budget BB, our goal is to select a subset 𝒮⊂𝒟pool\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pool}}, |𝒮|=B|\mathcal{S}|=B, that maximizes the model’s post-training performance on the target capability. We refer to this model as the student throughout the paper to denote the model being post-trained.

Ideally,

𝒮∗=arg⁡max𝒮⊂𝒟pool|𝒮|=B​𝒰target​(Train⁡(θ0,𝒮)),\mathcal{S}^{*}=\arg\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pool}}\\ |\mathcal{S}|=B\end{subarray}}\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{target}}\left(\operatorname{Train}(\theta_{0},\mathcal{S})\right), (1)

where 𝒰target\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{target}} denotes downstream performance on the target capability. Since evaluating this utility for candidate subsets would require repeated post-training, we instead optimize a tractable surrogate.

3.2 Target-Relevance Gate

We first restrict gradient-based selection to trajectories whose problems are semantically related to the target capability. Using a frozen embedding model ϕ\phi, we encode only the problem statements and rank candidates for each target reference by cosine similarity between their normalized embeddings. We construct a relevance gate 𝒢\mathcal{G} of fixed size G>BG>B by cycling through the target references and adding each reference’s highest-ranked unseen candidate until |𝒢|=G|\mathcal{G}|=G. This stage narrows the search space before applying the more expensive student-specific gradient analysis. Embedding similarity is used only to construct 𝒢\mathcal{G} and does not enter the final DeGMatch score. The resulting gate also defines the candidate population from which we estimate shared gradient structure in the next stage.

3.3 Deconfounded Gradient Geometry

Within 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we construct model-specific gradient representations for target-conditioned selection. Prior work on representation geometry shows that a shared mean and a small number of dominant principal directions can disproportionately shape pairwise similarity, and that removing these common components can expose more discriminative variation (Mu et al., 2018). We find an analogous phenomenon in reasoning gradients: candidate gradients exhibit strongly concentrated population-level structure, while raw target-conditioned rankings remain highly similar across different target references, as detailed in Appendix B. This motivates removing dominant candidate-population structure before target matching.

Step 1. Gradient sketching.

Following prior gradient-based data selection and attribution methods that compress high-dimensional per-example gradients for scalable matching (Xia et al., 2024; Park et al., 2023), we compute the gradient of the token-averaged completion loss with respect to the initial student model and sketch it into a tractable representation:

gi=Sketch⁡(∇θ0ℒ​(zi,θ0)),g_{i}=\operatorname{Sketch}\left(\nabla_{\theta_{0}}\mathcal{L}(z_{i};\theta_{0})\right), (2)

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is computed over completion tokens. Target gradients gjtg_{j}^{t} are computed using the same student parameters and sketching operator. We use CountSketch (Charikar et al., 2002); implementation details are provided in Appendix A.3.

Step 2. Population centering.

We first subtract the mean gradient of the candidate population, so that candidate and target gradients are represented relative to the same population mean. We compute

μ=1|𝒢|​∑zi∈𝒢gi,g¯i=gi−μ,g¯jt=gjt−μ.\mu=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}|}\sum_{z_{i}\in\mathcal{G}}g_{i},\qquad\bar{g}_{i}=g_{i}-\mu,\qquad\bar{g}_{j}^{t}=g_{j}^{t}-\mu. (3)

This centering removes the shared population offset and allows the subsequent principal-component analysis to characterize dominant variation around that baseline. The same candidate-derived mean is applied to target gradients so that candidates and targets share the same centered representation, without using target examples to estimate population statistics.

Step 3. Dominant-component removal.

Let UkU_{k} contain the top kk orthonormal principal directions of the centered candidate gradients {g¯i:zi∈𝒢}\{\bar{g}_{i}:z_{i}\in\mathcal{G}\}. We remove this dominant subspace using

P⟂=I−Uk​Uk⊤,P_{\perp}=I-U_{k}U_{k}^{\top}, (4)

and transform both candidate and target gradients as

g~i=P⟂​g¯i,g~jt=P⟂​g¯jt.\tilde{g}_{i}=P_{\perp}\bar{g}_{i},\qquad\tilde{g}_{j}^{t}=P_{\perp}\bar{g}_{j}^{t}. (5)

Both μ\mu and UkU_{k} are estimated exclusively from the candidate gradients within 𝒢\mathcal{G}, without directly incorporating target gradients into the population statistics. As shown in Appendix B, raw gradient matching is weakly sensitive to changes in the supplied target references, whereas suppressing this dominant candidate-population subspace substantially increases target sensitivity. This transformation affects only the geometry used for data selection; training uses the original trajectories and standard gradients.

3.4 Target-Conditioned Gradient Matching

Given the deconfounded gradients, we first compute directional alignment with the target references, following prior gradient-based target matching (Xia et al., 2024; Min et al., 2026). For candidate ii, let 𝒩q​(i)\mathcal{N}_{q}(i) denote the qq target gradients with the highest cosine similarity, and define

di=1q​∑j∈𝒩q​(i)cos⁡(g~i,g~jt).d_{i}=\frac{1}{q}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{q}(i)}\cos(\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{g}_{j}^{t}). (6)

We additionally weight this alignment by the magnitude of the candidate gradient within the target-gradient subspace. Let T=[g~1t,…,g~Mt]T=[\tilde{g}_{1}^{t},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{M}^{t}], and let Q=orth⁡(T)Q=\operatorname{orth}(T) denote an orthonormal basis for its column span. We define

mi=‖Q⊤​g~i‖2.m_{i}=\left\|Q^{\top}\tilde{g}_{i}\right\|_{2}. (7)

The two terms are complementary: did_{i} captures directional agreement with target gradients, while mim_{i} captures the strength of the candidate update within the target-gradient subspace. The final score combines them multiplicatively:

si=di​mi,𝒮=TopBzi∈𝒢⁡si.s_{i}=d_{i}m_{i},\qquad\mathcal{S}=\operatorname{TopB}_{z_{i}\in\mathcal{G}}s_{i}. (8)

Implementation details are provided in Appendix A.3.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Data and Target References

We evaluate mathematics, science, and code using OpenR1-Math-220k (Open-R1 Team, 2025c) and the science and CodeForces-CoT portions of Open-R1 Mixture-of-Thoughts (Open-R1 Team, 2025a), yielding 93K, 53K, and 26K trajectories, respectively. Each target uses 50 disjoint reference problems paired with verified DeepSeek-R1 trajectories. Pool and reference-set construction, including contamination filtering, are detailed in Appendices A.1 and A.2.

4.2 Baselines

We compare DeGMatch against heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific data-selection methods. Random uniformly samples from the candidate pool. Length selects the longest trajectories, following prior work showing that response or reasoning-trace length provides a simple but strong signal for post-training data selection (Zhao et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026b; Guha et al., 2026; Min et al., 2026). MaxPPL selects examples with the highest student-model perplexity as a simple proxy for difficulty.

Target-aware baselines include representation-based RDS+ (Ivison et al., 2025), gradient-based LESS (Xia et al., 2024) and GIST (Min et al., 2026), and optimal-transport-based TAROT (Feng et al., 2025).

Reasoning-specific baselines include RSR (Yang et al., 2026d), which combines student token rank and surprisal; TEMP (Jin et al., 2026), which uses perturbation-based loss trajectories; and Select2Reason (Yang et al., 2026b), which uses student-relative difficulty and trajectory characteristics.11 1 For Select2Reason, we evaluate the released Select2Reason-Qwen-7B checkpoint (https://huggingface.co/cehao/Select2Reason-Qwen-7B). We use matched candidate pools, selection budgets, and downstream training recipes wherever applicable; full implementation and adaptation details are provided in Appendix A.4.

We additionally report the initial student model and OpenR1-Qwen-7B (Open-R1 Team, 2025d) as reference points; the latter is treated as a full-data reference rather than a budget-matched selection baseline.

4.3 Training Setup

Our primary student is open-r1/Qwen2.5-Math-7B-RoPE-300k (Open-R1 Team, 2025e), derived from Qwen2.5-Math-7B (Yang et al., 2024). All selected subsets are fine-tuned from the same initialization under an identical training recipe. For the semantic relevance stage of DeGMatch, we use Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025), and set the relevance-gate size to three times the final selection budget in the main experiments across all domains. We keep all DeGMatch selection hyperparameters fixed across domains without target-specific retuning. Full optimization and implementation details are provided in Appendix A.6.

4.4 Evaluation

For mathematical reasoning, we build on the evaluation setting used in Select2Reason (Yang et al., 2026b) and evaluate on AIME24, AIME25, and AIME26 (Mathematical Association of America, 2025a), AMC23 (Mathematical Association of America, 2025b), HMMT Feb. 2025 (MathArena, 2025), MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024), and Gaokao 2024–2025 (FrankieYao, ). For scientific reasoning and code generation, we follow the benchmark families used in OpenThoughts (Guha et al., 2026), evaluating on GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2024), the physics and chemistry portions of JEEBench (Arora et al., 2023), LiveCodeBench v6 (Jain et al., 2025), and CodeForces (Open-R1 Team, ). Full benchmark provenance, prompting, decoding, verification, and repeated-sampling protocols are provided in Appendix A.7.

5 Main Results

5.1 Target-Aware Mathematical Reasoning

Table 1 presents the main results on mathematical reasoning. For target-aware methods, each evaluation target uses its corresponding reference set described in Appendix A.2, whereas target-agnostic methods use a single selected subset across benchmarks.

Strong and consistent target-aware specialization.

DeGMatch achieves the highest aggregate performance among data-selection methods, with an average score of 60.73 across eight benchmarks and the best result on six of eight. It outperforms all budget-matched heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific baselines, as well as the released Select2Reason checkpoint (58.99). DeGMatch also compares favorably with the full-data OpenR1-Qwen-7B reference (58.80), despite selecting only 10K examples from the 93K-example pool, although this full-data comparison is not budget matched.

Existing target-aware signals transfer imperfectly to reasoning.

Prior target-aware methods such as LESS, RDS+, GIST, and TAROT do not consistently outperform the strong Length baseline in our reasoning setting. LESS, GIST, and TAROT require an auxiliary warm-up or adaptation stage in our implementations, whereas DeGMatch operates directly on gradients from the initial student. These results suggest that target-aware signals developed primarily for instruction tuning do not transfer uniformly to long reasoning trajectories.

Target-specific utility goes beyond length and difficulty.

Length and MaxPPL remain strong baselines, showing that trajectory length and student difficulty provide useful selection signals. Reasoning-specific methods such as RSR, TEMP, and Select2Reason also perform competitively, yet DeGMatch achieves the strongest aggregate performance while using substantially fewer training tokens than Length and MaxPPL. These results suggest that effective target-specific selection benefits from signals beyond coarse proxies such as trajectory length or difficulty.

5.2 Generalization Beyond Mathematical Reasoning

We next examine whether DeGMatch generalizes beyond mathematics by applying the same selection procedure and hyperparameters to scientific reasoning and code generation. We select 5K science trajectories and 3K code trajectories and compare against Random and the strongest applicable baseline from each category in our mathematical experiments: Length, RDS+, and TEMP for heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific selection, respectively.22 2 Select2Reason is not included because only its released mathematical checkpoint is available; its selected data and selection pipeline are not publicly available for applying the method to science or code.

Consistent performance across reasoning domains.

DeGMatch is the strongest or tied-strongest subset-selection method on all four benchmarks without domain-specific retuning. The relative strength of competing signals varies across domains: Length remains competitive on science but degrades on code, RDS+ performs strongly on JEE, and TEMP matches DeGMatch on LiveCodeBench. In contrast, DeGMatch remains consistently strong across both science and code, suggesting that combining target relevance with student-specific gradient utility transfers across different reasoning domains.

Data efficiency persists beyond mathematics.

Despite using substantially less training data than full fine-tuning, DeGMatch matches or exceeds it on GPQA-D and LiveCodeBench, remains close on JEE, and trails on CodeForces. These results show that target-aware selection remains effective beyond mathematical reasoning with substantially reduced training volume.

6 Analysis

We analyze DeGMatch through component ablations, budget scaling, and cross-model robustness. Unless otherwise specified, analyses use a 3K budget and evaluate on AIME24, AIME25, AIME26, and AMC23 using the same 30K AIME relevance gate; Appendix C.1 separately varies the gate size. We compare against Random, Length, RDS+, and TEMP as representative reference, heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific baselines, respectively.

6.1 Component Validation

We examine the contributions of target relevance, candidate-population deconfounding, and the two terms of the final matching score. Table 3 summarizes the results, with detailed variant definitions provided in Appendix E.1.

Target relevance provides a useful first-stage signal.

Relevance-only selection improves over Random, showing that semantic relevance provides a useful signal for identifying target-relevant reasoning trajectories. Its average performance remains below the gradient-based variants and the full method, indicating that relevance alone does not capture student-specific training utility.

Deconfounding improves gradient matching.

Population centering improves over raw-gradient directional matching on average, and removing the dominant principal directions provides a further gain. This trend is consistent with the diagnostics in Appendix B, where suppressing dominant candidate-population structure increases the sensitivity of gradient rankings to the supplied target references.

Direction and magnitude provide complementary signals.

Neither deconfounded directional alignment nor target-subspace magnitude alone matches the full method, while their combination achieves the strongest average performance. Direction captures compatibility with target gradients, whereas magnitude measures the strength of the candidate update within the target-gradient subspace.

6.2 Data Efficiency Across Selection Budgets

We vary the selection budget from 1K to 15K trajectories and report average performance over AIME24, AIME25, and AIME26 as a function of both the number of selected examples and the resulting training-token volume in Figure 3.

DeGMatch remains effective across all selection budgets, matching or outperforming the strongest baselines at each scale and achieving its largest advantage at 10K examples, where it also surpasses the full-data reference (41.37 vs. 39.4). The token-based view further shows that these gains are not explained by selecting longer trajectories, as DeGMatch maintains a favorable performance–token trade-off relative to Length and RDS+. Overall, the budget sweep shows that the advantage of DeGMatch is not confined to a particular subset size and that strong performance can be achieved with substantially less training data than full-data training.

6.3 Robustness Across Student Models

Finally, we test whether DeGMatch transfers beyond the primary 7B student using three settings: Qwen2.5-3B-Base (Qwen Team, 2025) tests scaling within the same model family, Qwen3-1.7B-Base (Yang et al., 2025) introduces a different Qwen generation at a smaller scale, and Phi-3.5-mini-Instruct (Microsoft, 2024) provides a cross-family comparison with a different pretraining and instruction-tuning recipe. For each student, we recompute candidate and target gradients and independently select a model-specific subset under the same 3K budget. We exclude TEMP because it requires a parameter-compatible trained endpoint for each student.

Across these settings, DeGMatch remains consistently competitive and achieves the strongest overall performance on two of the three students. Its advantage also does not come from selecting substantially longer trajectories, as it uses fewer training tokens than Length and RDS+ across all three models. These results suggest that the selection principle is not specific to the primary 7B student and transfers across changes in model scale, generation, and family.

7 Conclusion

We study target-aware reasoning data selection, where a small reference set specifies a target capability to guide the selection of training trajectories. We introduce DeGMatch, which combines target-relevant retrieval with model-specific gradient matching in a deconfounded gradient space. By centering gradients and suppressing dominant candidate-population principal directions, DeGMatch reduces the influence of dominant population-level structure that can obscure target-dependent variation during gradient matching. Across mathematics, science, and code, DeGMatch achieves strong performance against heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific baselines while remaining effective across selection budgets, model families, and scales, supporting deconfounded gradient matching for target-aware reasoning data selection.

Limitations

Despite the effectiveness of DeGMatch, several directions remain open. First, our experiments focus on small- to medium-scale student models, and the scalability of student-gradient-based selection to substantially larger models remains to be studied. Second, we consider selection from existing reasoning-trajectory pools; jointly optimizing data generation, evolution, and selection may further improve post-training efficiency. Finally, while our analysis shows that removing dominant shared gradient structure improves target-conditioned matching, understanding what these gradient directions represent in terms of reasoning skills and behaviors remains an open question for future work.

Appendix A Experimental Details

A.1 Candidate-Pool Construction

Table 5 summarizes the candidate pools used in our experiments. We retain at most one reasoning trajectory per problem in all domains. Token counts are measured using the student-model tokenizer over the complete training sequence. Problems for which no verified trajectory is obtained within the attempt budget are discarded and replaced by another randomly sampled eligible problem.

For OpenR1-Math-220k (Open-R1 Team, 2025c), we use the default split and retain the first verified DeepSeek-R1 trajectory associated with each problem. For Mixture-of-Thoughts (Open-R1 Team, 2025a), we retain one trajectory per problem using a fixed random seed. The resulting science and code pools contain 53,195 and 26,061 unique problems, respectively. No retained example exceeds the 32,768-token training context.

Contamination check.

We check each candidate pool against its corresponding evaluation benchmarks for both exact overlap and near-duplicate problems. We find no evaluation problems in the final candidate pools under our contamination criteria. This check is performed before data selection, so all selection methods operate on the same contamination-filtered candidate pool.

Analysis metadata.

For post-hoc analyses of the mathematical candidate pool, we use the subject and source metadata distributed with OpenR1-Math-220k. Subject categories are taken directly from the dataset-provided problem_type field, which contains Algebra, Geometry, Number Theory, Combinatorics, Logic and Puzzles, Calculus, Inequalities, and Other; we use these labels without remapping. We define the Olympiad indicator as whether the dataset-provided source field equals olympiads. This indicator reflects dataset provenance rather than an inferred measure of difficulty and does not include examples assigned to other contest-related source tags. These metadata are used only for post-hoc analysis of DeGMatch and do not enter its candidate scoring or selection.

A.2 Target-Reference Construction

Target references are constructed independently for each target capability from source sets separate from the corresponding evaluation set. For each target, we remove invalid examples and examples belonging to the evaluation set, and then randomly sample 50 reference problems from the remaining pool using a fixed random seed. Each sampled problem is paired with a verified reasoning trajectory generated by DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025). Table 6 summarizes the reference source and corresponding evaluation set for each target.

For mathematical and scientific references, generation uses temperature 0.60.6, top-p=0.95p=0.95, and a maximum generation length of 32,768 tokens. We retain the first generated trajectory whose final answer is verified against the reference answer. We allow up to eight generation attempts for AIME, six for HMMT, MATH500, AMC, and Gaokao, and four for GPQA and JEE. Code references are verified by executing the extracted program against available test cases.

AIME.

We use the gneubig/aime-1983-2024 collection (Neubig, ), which contains historical American Invitational Mathematics Examination problems spanning multiple decades. Reference problems are drawn from competitions through 2023, while evaluation uses later AIME editions.

AMC.

We use edev2000/amc12-full (edev2000, ), a collection of historical AMC 12A and 12B competition problems. We use problems from the 2018–2022 competitions as the reference source and evaluate on AMC 2023.

HMMT.

Historical HMMT problems are obtained from Omni-MATH (KbsdJames, ), a collection of competition-level mathematical problems from multiple sources. We use HMMT problems from this collection as references and evaluate on the February 2025 HMMT benchmark released through MathArena (MathArena, 2025).

MATH.

We use the training split of the MATH dataset (Hendrycks et al., 2021) as the reference source. MATH contains competition-style mathematical problems organized by subject and difficulty level. Evaluation is performed on MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024), with exact duplicate problems excluded from the reference pool.

Gaokao.

We use the English-language Gaokao 2023 mathematics collection (MARIO-Math-Reasoning, 2023) as the reference source. Gaokao is China’s national college-entrance examination and covers a broad range of high-school mathematics topics. Evaluation uses the 2024 and 2025 English-language mathematics sets from GaoKaoMath (FrankieYao, ).

GPQA.

We use problems from the non-Diamond portion of GPQA (Rein et al., 2024) as scientific-reasoning references. GPQA consists of graduate-level multiple-choice questions spanning physics, chemistry, and biology. We evaluate on the more challenging GPQA-Diamond subset.

JEE.

We construct references from physics and chemistry problems in JEE Main 2023–2024 using the GRAFITe JEE collection (Ruh AI, ). JEE Main is an Indian engineering entrance examination covering high-school-level physics, chemistry, and mathematics. Evaluation is performed on the physics and chemistry portions of JEEBench (Arora et al., 2023).

LiveCodeBench.

We use historical problems from LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025) released before September 2024 as references. LiveCodeBench is a continuously updated code-generation benchmark designed to reduce contamination from previously released programming problems. Evaluation uses version 6 problems released between January and April 2025.

CodeForces.

We use the training split of the Open-R1 CodeForces collection (Open-R1 Team, ) as the reference source and its disjoint test split for evaluation. Reference problems are restricted to non-interactive problems with official test cases and are excluded if they already occur in the Mixture-of-Thoughts code candidate pool.

Relevance gate.

We use Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025) as the frozen embedding model. Only the problem statement is embedded; reasoning trajectories and auxiliary instructions are excluded. Inputs are truncated to 2,048 tokens, left padded, and represented by the final-token hidden state followed by ℓ2\ell_{2} normalization.

For each target reference, we independently rank the complete candidate pool by cosine similarity. Starting from retrieval depth k=1k=1, we cycle through target references in a fixed order and consider the kk-th nearest candidate of each reference. A candidate is added only if it has not already been included in the gate; duplicates are skipped. We then advance to the next retrieval depth and repeat until the desired gate size is reached. We set the gate size to three times the final selection budget, corresponding to 30K candidates for mathematics, 15K for science, and 9K for code. Embedding similarity is used only to construct the gate and is discarded before gradient-based reranking.

A.3 DeGMatch Implementation

Gradient sketching.

Directly storing a full-parameter gradient for every trajectory is impractical. Prior scalable gradient-based methods therefore construct low-dimensional gradient features before similarity or influence estimation; for example, LESS uses an 8,192-dimensional Rademacher random projection (Xia et al., 2024), following the random-projection approach used in TRAK (Park et al., 2023). We follow this general practice but sketch the full-parameter gradients using CountSketch (Charikar et al., 2002). Specifically, each per-example gradient is projected to 16,384 dimensions using a fixed sketch shared across all candidate and target examples. Prompt tokens are masked, and the loss is averaged over completion tokens.

The sketch in Step 1 is a fixed computational compression applied uniformly to candidates and targets, whereas the projection in Step 3 is the candidate-dependent transformation that deliberately removes dominant population structure before matching.

Deconfounding.

The gradient mean and principal directions are estimated only from examples inside the relevance gate. We subtract the gate-gradient mean and remove the top 50 principal directions. The same mean and projection are subsequently applied to target gradients. The target references therefore do not determine which population-level directions are removed. Let

G=[g¯1⊤g¯|𝒢|⊤]∈ℝ|𝒢|×dG=\begin{bmatrix}\bar{g}_{1}^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \bar{g}_{|\mathcal{G}|}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{G}|\times d}

denote the matrix of centered candidate gradients. We compute G=L​Σ​R⊤G=L\Sigma R^{\top} and define the dominant gradient-space basis as Uk=R:,1:kU_{k}=R_{:,1:k}, i.e., the top kk right singular vectors of the centered candidate-gradient matrix.

Target matching.

For each transformed candidate gradient, we compute cosine similarity to all transformed target gradients and define directional alignment as the mean similarity to the five most aligned references; thus, q=5q=5 in Eq. 6 for all experiments. To compute target-subspace magnitude, we form

T=[g~1t,…,g~Mt]T=[\tilde{g}_{1}^{t},\ldots,\tilde{g}_{M}^{t}]

and obtain an orthonormal basis QQ for its column space. We then compute mi=‖Q⊤​g~i‖2m_{i}=\|Q^{\top}\tilde{g}_{i}\|_{2} and rank candidates using the unclamped product si=di​mis_{i}=d_{i}m_{i}. The top-BB candidates within the relevance gate are selected for training.

A.4 Baseline Implementation Details

We implement all baselines under a controlled comparison while preserving their published selection rules as closely as possible. Unless otherwise noted, candidate scoring uses the same initial student model θ0\theta_{0}, examples are formatted using the same chat template as downstream training, and student-model scores are computed over completion tokens only with sequences retained up to 32,768 tokens. All selected subsets are subsequently fine-tuned from the same initial student checkpoint using the common training recipe in Appendix A.6.

Table 7 summarizes the implementation source, preserved selection rule, and main adaptation used for each principal baseline.

A.4.1 Heuristic Baselines

Random.

We uniformly sample examples from a fixed random permutation of the candidate pool.

Length.

We rank trajectories by the number of student-tokenizer tokens in the complete training sequence and select the longest examples.

MaxPPL.

We compute the mean negative log-likelihood over completion tokens under the initial student model and select examples with the highest values.

A.4.2 Target-Aware Baselines

RDS+.

We reimplement RDS+ (Ivison et al., 2025) following the published procedure. The representation model is the same initial student checkpoint used for downstream training, Qwen2.5-Math-7B-RoPE-300k, without additional warmup or fine-tuning. Each candidate is formatted exactly as its training sequence, including the system prompt, problem, and complete reasoning trajectory in the student chat template; target references are formatted analogously using the reference problem and its verified reasoning trajectory.

We run a single bf16 forward pass over the full sequence, up to 32,768 tokens, and extract final-layer hidden states h1,…,hLh_{1},\ldots,h_{L}. Following RDS+, the sequence representation is the position-weighted mean

e⁡(z)=∑i=1Lwi​hi,wi=i∑j=1Lj,e(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{L}w_{i}h_{i},\qquad w_{i}=\frac{i}{\sum_{j=1}^{L}j}, (9)

computed in fp32 and subsequently ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized. Candidate–reference similarity is measured by cosine similarity. We aggregate the resulting rankings using round-robin retrieval: cycling through target references in a fixed order, each reference contributes its highest-ranked candidate not already selected until the budget is reached. This construction is deterministic, and selections at smaller budgets are prefixes of those at larger budgets.

Shared warmup and gradient extraction.

LESS (Xia et al., 2024), GIST (Min et al., 2026), and TAROT (Feng et al., 2025) require gradient features obtained after an auxiliary warmup or adaptation stage. To avoid introducing variation from independently trained warmup models, we use a shared LoRA warmup for these three baselines.

Starting from the initial student, we train a LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapter with rank 128, α=512\alpha=512, and dropout 0.1 on the query, key, value, and output projections, yielding 80.7M trainable parameters. The adapter is trained on a uniformly sampled 5% of the mathematical candidate pool (4,683 examples, seed 42) for four epochs using AdamW with learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999), ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, no weight decay, a linear schedule with 3% warmup, effective batch size 32, and bf16 precision. We save the adapter and optimizer state after every epoch, yielding checkpoints θ1,…,θ4\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{4}.

For every candidate and target-reference example, we compute the per-example gradient of the mean token-level cross-entropy over completion tokens with respect to the LoRA parameters, using batch size 1 and disabling dropout. Because the original instruction-tuning implementations operate on substantially shorter inputs, we retain complete sequences up to 32,768 tokens to accommodate long reasoning trajectories and match our downstream training context. Target references are represented as problem–reasoning-trajectory pairs.

Whenever a baseline requires random projection, we use a fixed Rademacher matrix

Π∈{−1,+1}8192×d,\Pi\in\{-1,+1\}^{8192\times d}, (10)

shared across checkpoints, candidates, and target references.

LESS.

Following LESS (Xia et al., 2024), candidate examples are represented using Adam-preconditioned gradients. For a candidate gradient g⁡(z,θi)g(z;\theta_{i}) at checkpoint θi\theta_{i}, we compute

Γ⁡(z,θi)=β1​mi+(1−β1)​g​(z,θi)β2​vi+(1−β2)​g​(z,θi)2+ϵ,\Gamma(z;\theta_{i})=\frac{\beta_{1}m_{i}+(1-\beta_{1})g(z;\theta_{i})}{\sqrt{\beta_{2}v_{i}+(1-\beta_{2})g(z;\theta_{i})^{2}+\epsilon}}, (11)

where (mi,vi)(m_{i},v_{i}) are the first- and second-moment optimizer states stored at checkpoint θi\theta_{i}. We project these features to 8,192 dimensions using Π\Pi.

For each checkpoint, target references use plain gradients with the same projection and are averaged within the target capability to obtain g¯it\bar{g}^{\,t}_{i}. We score each candidate using

sLESS(z)=∑i=14η¯icos(ΠΓ(z;θi),g¯it),s_{\mathrm{LESS}}(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{4}\bar{\eta}_{i}\cos\!\left(\Pi\Gamma(z;\theta_{i}),\bar{g}^{\,t}_{i}\right), (12)

where η¯i\bar{\eta}_{i} is the average learning rate during warmup epoch ii, and select the highest-scoring examples.

GIST.

Following GIST (Min et al., 2026), we use the first warmup checkpoint θ1\theta_{1} and plain LoRA gradients without Adam preconditioning or random projection. Let

G∈ℝM×dG\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d} (13)

stack the gradients of the MM target-reference examples. We eigendecompose the uncentered target-gradient Gram matrix,

G​G⊤=V​Λ​V⊤,GG^{\top}=V\Lambda V^{\top}, (14)

and retain the smallest rank rr explaining at least 95% of the total eigenvalue mass; across our mathematical targets, rr ranges from 34 to 37.

Candidate gradients are represented in the corresponding target-gradient subspace as

Ur⊤g=Λr−1/2Vr⊤(Gg),U_{r}^{\top}g=\Lambda_{r}^{-1/2}V_{r}^{\top}(Gg), (15)

which we compute directly from candidate–reference gradient inner products. Target references are represented by the corresponding coordinates Vr​Λr1/2V_{r}\Lambda_{r}^{1/2}. Each candidate is scored by its maximum cosine similarity to an individual target reference in this subspace, and we select the highest-scoring examples.

TAROT.

For TAROT (Feng et al., 2025), we follow the published method description; the released implementation does not provide an LLM-specific training pipeline. The influence feature for an example is the sum of its projected plain gradients across the four warmup checkpoints,

ϕ⁡(z)=∑i=14Π​g​(z,θi).\phi(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{4}\Pi g(z;\theta_{i}). (16)

We mean-center candidate and reference features and apply Cholesky whitening using their joint covariance, regularized by 10−5​I10^{-5}I, followed by ℓ2\ell_{2} normalization. Pairwise cost is the Euclidean distance between the resulting whitened features,

c⁡(z,z′)=‖ϕ^​(z)−ϕ^​(z′)‖2.c(z,z^{\prime})=\left\|\hat{\phi}(z)-\hat{\phi}(z^{\prime})\right\|_{2}. (17)

We use TAROT’s fixed-size selection procedure with the same final budget as DeGMatch. Candidates are added layer by layer, where layer ℓ\ell contains the ℓ\ell-th nearest candidate for each target reference. If adding a complete layer would exceed the budget, candidates in the final layer are ordered by their dual potentials under the optimal-transport problem between the provisional selected set and the reference set.

We solve the OT problem using entropic Sinkhorn iterations implemented with GeomLoss (Feydy et al., 2019), with blur 0.01 (ϵ=10−4\epsilon=10^{-4}), ϵ\epsilon-scaling 0.5, no debiasing, and uniform masses. Across our targets, the budget is reached after 218–250 layers, so the OT-based tie breaking affects fewer than 0.5% of selected examples. We do not use OT-based reweighting or automatic selection-size estimation.

A.4.3 Reasoning-Specific Baselines

Several reasoning-specific methods were originally evaluated under settings that differ from our one-trajectory-per-problem candidate pool. Where necessary, we preserve their trajectory-level scoring or selection rule but adapt the final selection to a global fixed budget over our candidate pool. We treat such implementations as faithful adaptations under a controlled comparison.

RSR.

We faithfully adapt Rank–Surprisal Ratio (RSR) (Yang et al., 2026d) using the authors’ released implementation as reference. For each completion token tt, let ptp_{t} denote the probability assigned by the initial student to the observed token and let rtr_{t} denote its rank under the next-token distribution. Following the published implementation, ranks are truncated at 100, and the trajectory score is

sRSR​(z)=∑t∈ymin⁡(rt,100)∑t∈y−logpt.s_{\mathrm{RSR}}(z)=\frac{\sum_{t\in y}\min(r_{t},100)}{\sum_{t\in y}-\log p_{t}}. (18)

Lower scores are preferred.

The original setting selects among multiple teacher trajectories associated with the same problem. Because our pool contains at most one trajectory per problem, we preserve the trajectory-level score but rank all candidates globally and select the lowest-scoring BB examples. Our implementation follows the released definition of token rank, rank truncation, and response-token boundaries. We use the official RankSurprisalRatio repository (https://github.com/UmeanNever/RankSurprisalRatio) at commit 59a7c4c as the implementation reference.

TEMP.

We faithfully adapt TEMP (Jin et al., 2026) using the authors’ official implementation. TEMP estimates difficulty, diversity, and learnability from losses measured under perturbed versions of the student model. We use the initial student as θ0\theta_{0} and open-r1/OpenR1-Distill-7B (Open-R1 Team, 2025b) as the endpoint model θf\theta_{f} defining the directional perturbation axis.

We first perform the random-perturbation stage used to identify difficult examples. Gaussian perturbations are cumulatively applied to all non-embedding parameters of θ0\theta_{0} at eight increasing perturbation levels. On a fixed 2K calibration subset, we select the perturbation checkpoint whose mean loss ratio relative to θ0\theta_{0}, measured over the first 100 completion tokens, falls in the prescribed range of [2,3][2,3] and is closest to 2.5. For each source in the mathematical pool, we then apply kk-means with k=2k=2 to these losses and retain the higher-loss cluster. This leaves 42,862 of the original 93,733 mathematical candidates.

For the retained candidates, we construct loss trajectories along the direction from θ0\theta_{0} to θf\theta_{f}. Let

e=θf−θ0‖θf−θ0‖2.e=\frac{\theta_{f}-\theta_{0}}{\|\theta_{f}-\theta_{0}\|_{2}}. (19)

Following the released perturbation procedure, we generate eight directional checkpoints with tensor-wise seeded perturbations along ee and record the mean loss over the first 1,000 completion tokens at each checkpoint. Each candidate is therefore represented by an eight-dimensional loss trajectory.

We then follow TEMP’s source-aware selection procedure. Source-level budgets are allocated from the published difficulty statistics, loss trajectories are clustered independently within each source using FAISS kk-means, and candidates within each cluster are prioritized by their loss reduction from the first to the final directional checkpoint. The number of clusters within each source is set to approximately one quarter of its allocated budget, following the released selection script.

The released implementation computes the source allocation through a routine that assumes increasing loss along the directional checkpoints. This assumption does not hold for our reasoning-tuned endpoint model, for which loss generally decreases toward θf\theta_{f}. We therefore compute source allocations directly from the published equations while preserving the remaining perturbation, clustering, and within-cluster selection procedure. The resulting mathematical subset contains 10,000 trajectories and 64.9M training tokens. We use the official TEMP-ICML repository (https://github.com/BigML-CS-UCLA/TEMP-ICML) at commit b2a08ec as the implementation reference. We apply the same TEMP procedure to the mathematical, scientific, and code candidate pools wherever the required endpoint-model scoring and downstream evaluation are available. Accordingly, we report TEMP on all mathematical, science and code benchmarks.

Select2Reason.

For Select2Reason (Yang et al., 2026b), the data-selection code and selected training data are not publicly available. We therefore evaluate the authors’ released cehao/Select2Reason-Qwen-7B checkpoint rather than reproducing its data-selection and fine-tuning pipeline. The released checkpoint is initialized from a RoPE-extended Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct model, whereas DeGMatch and our matched implementations start from Qwen2.5-Math-7B-RoPE-300k, which is derived from the base Qwen2.5-Math-7B model and has not undergone instruction or reasoning post-training. Select2Reason therefore begins from a more specialized mathematical instruction-tuned initialization in addition to using a larger selected training set. We treat it as an external reasoning-selection reference rather than a matched implementation under our common training recipe.

A.5 Extended Comparison of Data-Selection Methods

Table 8 summarizes representative data-selection methods along dimensions relevant to our setting, including target conditioning, reasoning-specific design, student dependence, selection signal, use of gradients, and auxiliary fitting. The comparison provides additional context for the reasoning-specific and target-aware selection methods discussed in Section 2.

Scope of the empirical baseline comparison.

Our main experiments are not intended to exhaustively reproduce every data-curation method listed in Table 8. Instead, we select representative baselines that span the principal selection signals most directly comparable to our fixed-pool supervised fine-tuning setting. The target-aware baselines cover representation-based retrieval (RDS+), optimizer-aware gradient alignment (LESS), target-gradient subspace matching (GIST), and optimal-transport-based influence matching (TAROT). The reasoning-specific comparisons cover student-relative token difficulty (RSR), perturbation-based loss dynamics (TEMP), and Select2Reason as a recent reasoning-specific selection reference. Other methods in Table 8 provide broader context but may rely on different supervision, training objectives, data-construction assumptions, or closely related selection signals. We therefore use the extended table to situate DeGMatch within the broader literature while focusing the controlled experiments on representative methods that admit the closest comparison under our candidate pools and training setup.

A.6 Training Details

Unless otherwise specified, subset experiments start from open-r1/Qwen2.5-Math-7B-RoPE-300k (Open-R1 Team, 2025e), derived from Qwen2.5-Math-7B (Yang et al., 2024). We perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning using FSDP with bfloat16 precision and gradient checkpointing. We use AdamW with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, a peak learning rate of 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, cosine decay, and 5% warmup. The global batch size is 32, and each subset is trained for five epochs with a maximum sequence length of 32,768 tokens. We apply completion-only loss to assistant-response tokens and do not use sequence packing.

The training sequence uses the Qwen chat format with the system message "You are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are a helpful assistant." All subset experiments use training seed 42 and evaluate the final checkpoint. For full-data fine-tuning, we follow the OpenR1 training recipe, using a learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, a global batch size of 128, and three training epochs. This recipe is used only for the full-data reference.

A.7 Evaluation Details

We use a maximum model and generation length of 32,768 tokens. Evaluation is performed with vLLM using the model’s chat template. Table 9 summarizes benchmark size and repeated-sampling settings.

The initial student is a pretrained Qwen2.5-Math-7B base checkpoint whose RoPE base frequency was increased to 300K to support a 32K context window; it has not undergone instruction or reasoning post-training. Under this zero-shot evaluation setup, 21.4% of its generations reach the 32K-token limit, and outputs frequently continue beyond an attempted answer with new problems or repetitive text. We therefore report its score as a reference for the initial student checkpoint rather than as a competitive reasoning baseline.

Benchmark provenance.

Our mathematical evaluation follows the core benchmark families used by Select2Reason (Yang et al., 2026b), rather than reproducing its benchmark suite exactly. We evaluate on AIME24/25/26, AMC23, MATH500, Gaokao 2024/25, and HMMT Feb. 2025. For science and code, we follow the benchmark families used in OpenThoughts (Guha et al., 2026), evaluating on GPQA-Diamond, the physics and chemistry portions of JEEBench, LiveCodeBench v6, and the Open-R1 CodeForces test split. Table 9 lists the corresponding benchmark citations and evaluation sizes. OpenThoughts additionally reports CodeElo (Quan et al., 2025); we omit it because its official evaluation protocol submits generated solutions directly to the Codeforces platform. We instead evaluate CodeForces solutions locally against the available official test cases.

Sampling variability.

Repeated sampling is particularly important for small competition benchmarks. Across our evaluated runs, the standard error of the sampled accuracy estimate is approximately 0.8–1.2 percentage points for AIME under Avg@16 and 1.0–1.1 points for AMC under Avg@16. The corresponding ranges are approximately 0.6–0.8 points for GPQA-Diamond under Avg@8 and 0.5–1.1 points for JEEBench under Avg@4. As an additional diagnostic, splitting the 16 AIME generations into two disjoint groups of eight can produce accuracy estimates differing by as much as 5.8 points. We therefore use Avg@16 for the small mathematical competition benchmarks to reduce generation-sampling noise. These statistics characterize evaluation-time sampling variability and should not be interpreted as variation across independently trained models.

For AIME, AMC, HMMT, GPQA, MATH500, Gaokao, and LiveCodeBench, generation uses temperature 0.60.6 and top-p=0.95p=0.95. The current JEEBench and CodeForces harnesses use temperature 0.70.7 and top-p=1.0p=1.0.

AIME and AMC answers are extracted from the final \boxed{} expression. HMMT uses the MathArena answer extraction and verification procedure. MATH500 and Gaokao are graded using math-verify. GPQA-Diamond is scored using exact multiple-choice accuracy after deterministic option shuffling. LiveCodeBench and CodeForces generations are executed against benchmark test cases.

A.8 Computational Resources and Cost

Hardware and DeGMatch selection cost.

All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q GPUs with 96 GB memory. Candidate-gradient features can be computed once for each student model and reused across target capabilities. For the primary student, computing projected gradients for the complete candidate pools requires approximately 58.3 GPU-hours for mathematics (93,733 examples), 16.4 GPU-hours for science (53,195 examples), and 35.1 GPU-hours for code (26,061 examples). Once the candidate features are available, computing gradients for a 50-example target-reference set requires at most 0.11 GPU-hours per target. Relevance-gate construction, PCA-based deconfounding, and final scoring require approximately five CPU minutes per mathematical target and are negligible relative to gradient extraction.

Selection-cost comparison.

Table 10 compares the approximate cost of constructing reusable selection features for the principal target-aware baselines and DeGMatch. All measurements correspond to our long-context implementations on RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. For LESS, GIST, and TAROT, the reported cost includes the auxiliary warm-up or adaptation used in our implementations together with candidate-gradient feature extraction. Candidate representations and warm-up checkpoints are reusable across targets for all applicable methods, so the comparison focuses on the one-time feature-construction cost rather than repeatedly charging shared computation for every target.

Under our implementation, DeGMatch requires roughly 29% of the selection compute used by LESS or TAROT and is comparable in cost to GIST, despite using full-parameter rather than LoRA gradients. Its main practical distinction is that it requires no auxiliary warm-up or adaptation checkpoint: the reusable candidate representation is computed directly from the initial student. RDS+ remains substantially cheaper because it requires only a forward pass. For DeGMatch, adding a new target after candidate features have been computed requires only the small target-gradient computation and several minutes of CPU-side retrieval, deconfounding, and scoring. The same reuse principle applies to reusable candidate features and warm-up checkpoints of the reproduced baselines.

Training cost.

Training cost depends substantially on the number of tokens contained in the selected subset. A 10K-example mathematical subset trained for five epochs typically requires approximately eight hours on the same eight-GPU node, corresponding to roughly 60–70 GPU-hours per run. Representative DeGMatch runs require approximately 7.8–8.4 hours, compared with 6.6 hours for Random and 9.5 hours for Length. This variation reflects differences in the total number and length of selected training tokens rather than differences in the optimization procedure. Science and code experiments use smaller example budgets and correspondingly shorter training runs.

Target-reference generation cost.

Constructing the target-reference sets requires generating verified reasoning trajectories for the sampled reference problems. Table 11 reports the token usage and monetary cost incurred during this process. Across all nine target capabilities, generating 450 verified reference trajectories uses approximately 5.20M output tokens and costs $12.75 in total, or about $1.42 per target on average. Thus, the monetary cost of constructing the small target-reference sets is modest relative to subsequent selection and fine-tuning compute. Reported monetary costs correspond to the API prices in effect when the reference trajectories were generated.

Appendix B Diagnosing Target-Conditioned Gradient Matching

We provide additional analysis of the gradient-matching limitation motivating the deconfounding step in Section 3.3. We examine two questions: (1) whether reasoning gradients contain dominant structure shared across the candidate population, and (2) whether this structure makes raw target-conditioned matching insufficiently sensitive to the supplied target references. We then analyze how candidate-population deconfounding changes this behavior.

Connection to common-component removal.

Mu et al. (2018) observe that learned representations can contain a nonzero population mean and a small number of dominant principal directions shared broadly across examples. Their All-but-the-Top transformation centers the representation population and removes its leading principal subspace:

xi′=(I−UD​UD⊤)​(xi−μx).x_{i}^{\prime}=(I-U_{D}U_{D}^{\top})(x_{i}-\mu_{x}). (20)

The key geometric observation is that directions explaining substantial population-level variation need not be the directions that best distinguish individual examples under similarity-based comparison. DeGMatch considers the analogous issue for student gradients: whether dominant structure shared across candidate trajectories can overwhelm the variation that distinguishes one target capability from another.

Why dominant components can reduce target sensitivity.

Population centering removes the common mean offset, whereas principal-component removal suppresses dominant variation around that mean. These operations address distinct aspects of the gradient geometry, and we evaluate their effects separately. Let U∈ℝd×kU\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} denote a dominant subspace of the centered candidate gradients. We can decompose a centered candidate gradient and target gradient as

g¯i=U​ai+ri,g¯jt=U​bjt+sjt,\bar{g}_{i}=Ua_{i}+r_{i},\qquad\bar{g}_{j}^{t}=Ub_{j}^{t}+s_{j}^{t}, (21)

where

U⊤​ri=0,U⊤​sjt=0.U^{\top}r_{i}=0,\qquad U^{\top}s_{j}^{t}=0. (22)

Their inner product therefore decomposes as

g¯i⊤​g¯jt=ai⊤​bjt+ri⊤​sjt.\bar{g}_{i}^{\top}\bar{g}_{j}^{t}=a_{i}^{\top}b_{j}^{t}+r_{i}^{\top}s_{j}^{t}. (23)

Correspondingly,

cos⁡(g¯i,g¯jt)=ai⊤​bjt+ri⊤​sjt‖ai‖22+‖ri‖22​‖bjt‖22+‖sjt‖22.\cos(\bar{g}_{i},\bar{g}_{j}^{t})=\frac{a_{i}^{\top}b_{j}^{t}+r_{i}^{\top}s_{j}^{t}}{\sqrt{\|a_{i}\|_{2}^{2}+\|r_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}\sqrt{\|b_{j}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}+\|s_{j}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}}}. (24)

If a high-energy subspace captures broad properties shared across candidate and reference trajectories, its contribution ai⊤​bjta_{i}^{\top}b_{j}^{t} can dominate pairwise similarity even when those properties are not specific to the target capability of interest. In this case, references that match such broad trajectory properties can induce candidate rankings similar to those produced by the true target references, thereby obscuring finer target-conditioned variation in the matching geometry.

After removing the dominant candidate subspace,

P⟂​g¯i=ri,P⟂​g¯jt=sjt,P_{\perp}\bar{g}_{i}=r_{i},\qquad P_{\perp}\bar{g}_{j}^{t}=s_{j}^{t}, (25)

and cosine matching depends only on the residual geometry:

cos⁡(P⟂​g¯i,P⟂​g¯jt)=ri⊤​sjt‖ri‖2​‖sjt‖2.\cos(P_{\perp}\bar{g}_{i},P_{\perp}\bar{g}_{j}^{t})=\frac{r_{i}^{\top}s_{j}^{t}}{\|r_{i}\|_{2}\|s_{j}^{t}\|_{2}}. (26)

This argument does not require the removed directions to be uninformative for optimization. A direction can contain substantial gradient energy while still being poorly suited for distinguishing target identity if it is shared broadly across candidates and targets. DeGMatch therefore removes these directions only from the geometry used for selection; training on the selected trajectories uses the original supervision and the full model gradients.

This argument yields two empirical predictions. First, candidate gradients should contain a high-energy population-level subspace that strongly determines raw gradient rankings. Second, if this subspace captures broad trajectory properties rather than target content alone, non-target references matched on such properties should reproduce much of the raw candidate ordering, and this dependence should be reduced specifically by removing the dominant directions. We test these predictions below.

B.1 Dominant Shared Structure in Candidate Gradients

We first test whether the concentration of reasoning gradients into a small number of dominant directions is specific to a particular target-conditioned candidate population. Table 12 reports the cumulative variance explained by the leading principal components after centering each of the five mathematical relevance gates by its own candidate-population mean. The spectra are consistently concentrated across targets: the first 10 components explain 78.2–82.6% of the variance, and the first 50 explain 86.7–89.4%. Thus, the dominant-spectrum phenomenon observed for AIME is not specific to a single relevance gate.

To characterize what varies along these directions, Table 13 reports absolute Spearman correlations between scores along the leading PCs and several trajectory-level properties. PC1 is strongly associated with gradient norm (|ρ|=0.86|\rho|=0.86), while PC1 and PC2 are also associated with trajectory length and student NLL. In contrast, source and problem-type indicators exhibit substantially weaker associations with the dominant components. These correlations are descriptive and do not imply that trajectory length, NLL, or gradient norm causes the dominant structure.

Figure 4 provides a complementary visualization of these diagnostics. The spectrum is strongly concentrated, while the scatter plots and correlation summary show that the leading components are associated with broad trajectory-level quantities such as gradient magnitude, sequence length, and student NLL. Together with Tables 12 and 13, this indicates that raw gradient similarity is computed in a space containing substantial candidate-population structure shared across many trajectories.

We additionally compare how much gradient energy candidate and target examples allocate to the dominant candidate subspace. Table 14 reports the fraction of squared centered-gradient norm captured by its first kk principal directions. At k=50k=50, 86.1% of the energy of randomly sampled gate gradients lies in this subspace, compared with 77.7%, 80.5%, and 78.1% for AIME, AMC, and HMMT target references, respectively.

We next ask whether the dominant directions recur across different target-conditioned candidate populations. A direct comparison of the relevance gates is potentially confounded by shared candidates, so we construct a stricter control in which each target retains only candidates that appear in no other target’s gate. We then recompute PCA independently on these mutually exclusive candidate sets.

For two kk-dimensional principal subspaces with orthonormal bases UU and VV, we measure normalized subspace overlap as

overlap⁡(U,V)=1k​∥U⊤​V∥F2.\operatorname{overlap}(U,V)=\frac{1}{k}\lVert U^{\top}V\rVert_{F}^{2}.

This quantity equals one for identical subspaces and approaches zero for unrelated low-dimensional subspaces.

As shown in Table 15, the dominant directions remain strongly aligned even under this zero-overlap construction. The first five components have a mean cross-target subspace overlap of 0.93, nearly matching the 0.94 overlap obtained from non-overlapping random subsets of the same underlying mathematical pool. The first 50 components also remain substantially aligned (0.79 versus a 0.87 pool-split reference), whereas components 51–100 are markedly less shared (0.45 versus 0.60). Thus, the strongest population-level directions recur across target-conditioned candidate populations even when their underlying examples do not overlap. We emphasize that these candidate gates are not themselves ground-truth samples from the downstream tasks; this analysis characterizes shared structure in the candidate populations induced by different target references.

Together, these results establish two properties of the candidate-gradient geometry: its variance is strongly concentrated in a small number of leading directions across targets, and these dominant directions recur across distinct target-conditioned candidate populations. We next examine whether this shared high-variance structure interferes with target-conditioned gradient matching.

B.2 Why Remove the Dominant Principal Directions?

The preceding analysis establishes that candidate gradients contain strong population-level structure, but high variance alone does not justify removing the corresponding directions. We therefore ask a more direct question: does this structure cause target-conditioned gradient matching to respond to broad trajectory properties rather than to the target references themselves?

A matched non-target control.

We construct a negative control for the AIME target by replacing each AIME reference with a non-target trajectory outside the AIME relevance gate that is closely matched in trajectory length and student NLL. We repeat this construction with three random seeds. The candidate population is held fixed to the same 30K AIME relevance gate used by DeGMatch. Unless otherwise noted, the diagnostics in this subsection use the directional matching score did_{i}, so that they isolate the similarity geometry affected by deconfounding.

Raw gradient matching fails this negative-control test: the ranking induced by the true AIME references is largely reproduced by the matched non-target references (mean Spearman ρ=0.86\rho=0.86). Thus, much of the raw candidate ordering can be recovered from references that match broad trajectory statistics without specifying the intended target capability.

Raw rankings are dominated by population structure.

To identify the source of this behavior, we decompose each gradient into the component contained in the dominant candidate-population space and its orthogonal residual. The dominant component consists of the population mean together with the top 50 principal directions estimated from the centered 30K gate gradients. Across the five mathematical targets, rankings computed using only this dominant component correlate with the corresponding raw rankings at ρ=0.96\rho=0.96–0.990.99; for AIME, the correlation is 0.990.99 and the top-10% overlap is 0.850.85. In contrast, rankings computed from the residual component alone correlate with the raw rankings at only 0.010.01–0.280.28. The same dominance is observed with randomly sampled reference trajectories, for which the dominant component still reproduces the raw ranking with ρ=0.96\rho=0.96.

Figure 5 visualizes this decomposition and the negative-control test. The result does not imply that the leading components contain no target-related information. Rather, it shows that the raw matching geometry is dominated by population-level structure through which broad reference properties can strongly determine the candidate ordering.

The effect is specific to the leading directions.

A possible alternative explanation is that matching improves simply because 50 dimensions are removed. We test this by removing the same number of directions from different parts of the gradient space after population centering. Removing 50 random orthogonal directions, PCs 51–100, or PCs 151–200 leaves the matched-control correlation essentially unchanged at ρ≈0.87\rho\approx 0.87. Only removal of PCs 1–50 reduces it substantially, to 0.280.28. The same intervention also reduces correlation with rankings induced by random reference sets. These controls show that the effect is not a generic consequence of dimensionality reduction, but is specific to suppressing the dominant candidate-population directions.

B.3 Can Measured Covariates Explain the Confounding?

The analyses above show that the dominant gradient directions are associated with broad trajectory properties such as sequence length, student NLL, and gradient magnitude. This raises a simpler alternative: rather than estimating and removing dominant population structure, could we directly regress out these measured properties?

We test this possibility in the same fixed 30K AIME relevance gate. We consider three alternatives to principal-component removal. First, we residualize the raw directional matching score using a linear regression on log trajectory length, student NLL, and log gradient norm. Second, we use a cubic polynomial expansion with interaction terms. Third, we regress the same covariates directly from the gradient representations before computing directional matching. Table 16 reports the resulting diagnostics.

Explicit covariate correction substantially reduces the direct association between the matching score and trajectory length: the score–length correlation changes from 0.720.72 for raw matching to between −0.11-0.11 and −0.17-0.17 after score- or gradient-level residualization. Nevertheless, the negative-control dependence remains strong. The length- and NLL-matched non-target references still reproduce the resulting candidate rankings with correlations of 0.700.70–0.790.79, compared with 0.280.28 after removing the dominant candidate PCs.

This difference indicates that eliminating the marginal dependence on a few measured trajectory statistics is not sufficient to remove the population structure that dominates raw matching. Consistent with this interpretation, removing the top 50 PCs after gradient-level covariate residualization further lowers the matched-control correlation to 0.240.24, only slightly below PC removal alone. Moreover, the top-50 principal subspaces estimated before and after covariate residualization have a projection overlap of 0.970.97. Thus, the dominant candidate subspace appears to subsume variation associated with length, NLL, and gradient scale while also capturing additional shared multidimensional structure that is not specified by these measured covariates.

B.4 Shared Structure and Reasoning-Trajectory Length

We finally examine whether the shared population structure is associated with the long trajectories characteristic of reasoning post-training. We compare instruction-tuning examples from the LESS data pool, short mathematical solutions from MATH, and long R1 reasoning trajectories using the same student model, gradient extraction procedure, and CountSketch representation.

Table 17 shows that the clearest difference appears in the shared mean direction rather than in the centered PCA spectrum. For instruction-tuning examples, the mean direction accounts for only 1.6%1.6\% of gradient energy and the average sample-to-mean cosine is −0.02-0.02. For long R1 reasoning trajectories, the corresponding values increase to 43.8%43.8\% and 0.710.71, respectively. Short mathematical solutions lie between these settings, with 10.0%10.0\% mean-direction energy and a sample-to-mean cosine of 0.400.40, suggesting that the strong shared structure observed for R1 trajectories is not attributable to the mathematical domain alone. Consistently, raw reasoning-gradient rankings are substantially more reproducible under random reference sets than instruction-tuning rankings (ρ=0.75\rho=0.75 vs. 0.350.35).

To examine the association with trajectory length more directly, we recompute gradients for a fixed subset of up to 2,000 reasoning examples after truncating their responses to 256, 1,024, and 4,096 tokens. As shown in Figure 6, mean-direction energy increases from 3%3\% at 256 tokens to 17%17\% at 1,024 tokens and 42%42\% at 4,096 tokens, reaching 46%46\% for the full trajectories. The same pattern appears in the unmodified reasoning data: across trajectory-length deciles, sample-to-mean alignment increases with length and plateaus for the longest trajectories (Spearman ρ=0.65\rho=0.65).

Together, these results are consistent with shared gradient structure becoming more prominent as reasoning trajectories grow longer. We treat this analysis as evidence consistent with a length-related mechanism rather than as causal identification of trajectory length as the sole source of the shared population structure.

B.5 Target Sensitivity of Existing Target-Aware Selectors

We first examine the selected subsets produced by existing target-aware methods. For each selector, we independently obtain 10K-example subsets for AIME, AMC, HMMT, MATH500, and Gaokao and compute the pairwise Jaccard similarity

J⁡(St,St′)=|St∩St′||St∪St′|J(S_{t},S_{t^{\prime}})=\frac{|S_{t}\cap S_{t^{\prime}}|}{|S_{t}\cup S_{t^{\prime}}|}

between the resulting target-specific subsets. We additionally include TSDS (Liu et al., 2024b) as an auxiliary target-aware comparison for this diagnostic.

Figure 7 shows that target sensitivity varies substantially across methods. LESS, GIST, and TSDS produce highly overlapping subsets across targets, with mean pairwise Jaccard similarities of 0.64, 0.52, and 0.42, respectively. For comparison, two independently sampled uniform 10K subsets from the 93,733-example mathematical pool have an expected Jaccard similarity of approximately 0.056. The corresponding pairwise matrices show that the high averages are not driven by a single target pair: LESS and GIST in particular retain substantial overlap across most target combinations.

RDS+ and TAROT exhibit stronger differentiation across targets, with mean Jaccard similarities of 0.19 and 0.11, respectively, while DeGMatch yields 0.15. Thus, the diagnostic does not imply that all existing target-aware methods are insensitive to target identity. Rather, it shows that the extent to which selected data respond to the supplied target varies substantially across existing methods.

Importantly, lower overlap is not itself a measure of selection quality. TAROT produces even lower cross-target overlap than DeGMatch, yet does not outperform the strongest target-agnostic baselines in downstream evaluation. We therefore use cross-target overlap only as a diagnostic of how strongly a selector responds to target identity, rather than as an objective that should be minimized.

B.6 Additional Target-Sensitivity Diagnostics

As a complementary diagnostic, we also examine how rankings and selected subsets vary across the five mathematical target reference sets. These cross-target comparisons should not be interpreted as a direct measure of selection quality: lower overlap is not intrinsically better, and different targets may legitimately share useful training examples.

Table 18 reports two complementary diagnostics. Matched-control ρ\rho is the Spearman correlation between the AIME-conditioned ranking and a ranking obtained after replacing the AIME references with a non-target control matched for trajectory length and student NLL. The remaining columns measure the intersection fraction between equal-size top-10K subsets,

O⁡(St,St′)=|St∩St′|10,000,O(S_{t},S_{t^{\prime}})=\frac{|S_{t}\cap S_{t^{\prime}}|}{10{,}000},
