after replacing the AIME references with AMC, HMMT, MATH500, or Gaokao references. This differs from the Jaccard similarity used in Section B.5: here the denominator is the fixed selection budget rather than the union size. These quantities are diagnostics of target dependence rather than performance metrics; lower overlap is not intrinsically better.

Raw gradient matching is strikingly insensitive to target replacement. Replacing the AIME references with the matched non-target control preserves a ranking correlation of 0.860.86, while replacing them with another mathematical target retains 89–96% of the raw top-10K set. Population centering changes the cross-target rankings but leaves matched-control correlation essentially unchanged at 0.870.87, indicating that mean removal alone does not resolve the target-insensitivity captured by this diagnostic.

Removing the dominant candidate principal directions produces a qualitatively different geometry. With k=50k=50, matched-control correlation falls from 0.86 to 0.28, while the cross-target top-10K intersection fraction falls to 0.56–0.78. The resulting rankings also preserve non-uniform relationships among targets: AIME remains more similar to AMC and HMMT than to MATH500 or Gaokao. Thus, dominant-component removal makes the candidate ranking substantially more dependent on which target references are supplied, rather than merely applying a target-independent perturbation.

Figure 8 visualizes this effect while holding the candidate population fixed. The left panel tracks ranking similarity to the matched non-target control as progressively more of the dominant candidate subspace is removed. Mean-centering alone leaves the correlation essentially unchanged, whereas removing the leading principal directions produces a sharp reduction. This distinction is important: although centering changes the overall similarity geometry, the dominant variation around the mean remains sufficient for a matched non-target reference set to induce nearly the same candidate ordering as the true target.

The right panel measures the mean pairwise top-10K overlap among all five mathematical targets while every target scores the same 30K AIME gate. Raw matching produces an overlap of 0.93, indicating that different target references induce almost identical selections. Mean-centering substantially reduces this average overlap, while the pairwise matrices reveal that several target pairs remain highly similar. Removing the dominant principal directions further changes the target-conditioned ranking structure while sharply reducing the matched-control correlation in the left panel.

The last matrix in Figure 8 additionally shows the final DeGMatch subsets when each target uses its own relevance gate. Their overlap is lower still, illustrating that the two stages provide complementary sources of target differentiation: semantic retrieval first restricts selection to a target-relevant candidate region, while deconfounded gradient matching makes the subsequent reranking within that region more responsive to the supplied target. This distinction also separates the effect of gradient deconfounding from the additional target specificity contributed by the relevance gate.

Importantly, this effect is not equivalent to removing trajectory-length information. The final DeGMatch score remains correlated with trajectory length (ρ=0.69\rho=0.69 at k=50k=50), and the magnitude term explicitly preserves information about update strength. The role of deconfounding is therefore narrower: reducing target-insensitive population structure that dominates matching while retaining other signals that can remain useful for selection.

B.7 Target Structure in Rankings Induced by Reference Subsets

The analyses above show that removing dominant candidate-population structure makes rankings more responsive to changes in the supplied target references. We next ask whether this increased sensitivity reveals target-dependent structure rather than arbitrary dispersion.

For each of the five mathematical targets, we partition the reference set into disjoint 10-example subsets and independently compute the candidate ranking induced by each subset. We repeat the partitioning multiple times and score the same fixed 30K AIME relevance gate in every case, so changes in the ranking geometry cannot be attributed to changes in the candidate population. Distances between two induced rankings are defined as one minus their Spearman correlation.

Figure 9 decomposes the effect of deconfounding step by step. Under raw gradients, target identity can be recovered from an induced ranking with 56% accuracy, compared with a 20% five-way chance level. Population centering alone changes this only marginally to 57%. Likewise, retaining only the top 50 principal components of the centered gradients yields 56% target identification. In contrast, removing the population mean and these dominant components increases target identification to 71%.

For target identification, each reference-subset query is assigned to the target whose other disjoint reference subsets have the highest average Spearman correlation with its induced ranking. The identification score is therefore measured directly in the original candidate-ranking space, rather than from the two-dimensional visualization.

The close behavior of the centered and dominant-subspace representations further indicates that mean removal alone does not eliminate the dominant population variation. Across the reference-subset queries, rankings produced after centering and rankings produced using only the top-50 principal-component subspace have Spearman correlations of 0.997–0.999, with 94–96% overlap among their top-3K candidates. Thus, most of the target-conditioned ranking geometry that remains after centering is still carried by the dominant candidate directions.

Importantly, the dominant subspace is not devoid of target information: it retains coarse relationships among the mathematical targets. The relevant observation is instead that suppressing this high-energy population structure makes finer target identity more recoverable from the resulting candidate ordering. This supports the interpretation that dominant shared directions can obscure, rather than completely eliminate, target-dependent variation.

B.8 Visualizing Target-Conditioned Selection

We further visualize how deconfounding changes which candidates are highly ranked across targets. Figure 10 plots the top-1K candidates selected for each of the five mathematical targets under raw-gradient matching and after deconfounding.

Raw-gradient matching concentrates the target-conditioned selections on a small common set. Across the five top-1K lists, the union contains only 1,317 distinct candidates. Among these distinct candidates, 54.0% are selected by all five targets and 74.1% are selected by at least three targets. After deconfounding, the union expands to 2,950 distinct candidates; among these, only 2.4% are selected by all five targets and 17.4% by at least three. These statistics directly quantify the reduction in repeated selection of the same candidates across targets.

Together with the controlled ranking diagnostics above, this visualization shows the same phenomenon at the level of selected candidates: raw gradient matching repeatedly favors a common set across targets, whereas deconfounding produces substantially more target-dependent selections.

B.9 Number of Removed Components

We use k=50k=50 principal directions in the main experiments. Table 19 summarizes how the representation-level diagnostics change as kk varies. Increasing kk steadily reduces correlation with the matched non-target control, with the largest change occurring within the first several dozen removed directions. The total number of training tokens in the resulting 10K subsets remains comparatively stable across these settings.

Figure 11 provides a complementary ranking-level view of this sensitivity. The increase in target discrimination is not specific to the default choice of k=50k=50. Across k=5k=5–150150, removing the dominant components yields target-identification accuracy between 66% and 82%, compared with 56% for raw gradients and 57% after centering alone. In contrast, rankings formed using only the corresponding leading components remain substantially less target-discriminative over the evaluated values. Removing only two components is insufficient and reduces identification to 44%, suggesting that the relevant shared structure extends beyond the very first directions.

Together with the matched-control diagnostic in Table 19, these results indicate that the qualitative effect of dominant-component removal is robust over a broad range of kk rather than arising from a narrowly tuned choice. We retain k=50k=50 as the fixed operating point because it lies within this stable regime and gives the strongest downstream average among the evaluated settings.

The matched-control correlation decreases from 0.39 at k=10k=10 to 0.28 at k=50k=50, after which the improvement becomes more gradual. Meanwhile, selected-token volume remains within 96–99M tokens across all settings. We therefore use k=50k=50 as a fixed operating point: the largest changes in target sensitivity occur within the first several dozen components, while further removal produces progressively smaller changes and the selected-token volume remains stable.

Downstream sensitivity to the number of removed components.

The representation-level diagnostics above show that suppressing additional dominant components progressively reduces sensitivity to the matched non-target control. We additionally test whether the choice of kk materially affects downstream performance. Using the fixed 3K analysis budget and otherwise identical selection and training settings, we vary the number of removed principal components and evaluate the resulting models on AIME24, AIME25, and AIME26. Table 20 reports the results, where k=0k=0 denotes population centering without principal-component removal.

Downstream performance is relatively stable across a broad range of component-removal settings, while removing the top 50 components achieves the strongest average performance among the evaluated values of kk. In particular, the average improves from 34.00 with centering alone to 34.83 at k=50k=50, while both smaller and larger removal sizes remain competitive. Together with the representation-level diagnostics above, these results support k=50k=50 as a fixed operating point rather than a target-specific tuned hyperparameter. We use the same value across all targets and domains.

B.10 Estimating Population Structure Within the Relevance Gate

Our default implementation estimates the mean and principal directions from all examples inside the relevance gate. Table 21 compares this choice with subsampled and full-pool alternatives.

Estimating the subspace from 6K randomly sampled gate examples changes approximately 10–13% of the selected subset, while estimating it from the full mathematical pool produces a subset with 0.88 overlap with the default. DeGMatch defines the dominant population structure relative to the candidate population being reranked. Estimating this structure from a small random subset introduces additional sampling variability, whereas estimating it from the full pool incorporates variation outside the target-relevant candidate region. We therefore estimate the mean and principal directions from the complete relevance gate.

B.11 Directional-Alignment Statistics

Finally, we examine a potential edge case of the multiplicative DeGMatch score. The directional term did_{i} in Eq. 6 is an average cosine similarity and can therefore be negative. Because DeGMatch uses the unclamped score si=di​mis_{i}=d_{i}m_{i}, a sufficiently large magnitude could in principle change the ordering among negatively aligned candidates. Table 22 reports the relevant statistics for every target used in our main experiments.

At least 98.6% of gated candidates have positive directional alignment in every setting, and the number of positively aligned candidates substantially exceeds the selection budget. More importantly, every trajectory selected by DeGMatch has di>0d_{i}>0, with the minimum selected value ranging from 0.014 to 0.025.

As a direct check, replacing the implemented score with si=max⁡(di,0)​mis_{i}=\max(d_{i},0)m_{i} produces exactly the same selected subset for every target. Thus, although the unclamped product admits a theoretical ordering ambiguity among negatively aligned candidates, negative alignment does not affect any selection or downstream result reported in this work.

Appendix C Analysis of the Relevance Gate

We analyze how the relevance gate shapes the candidate region before gradient-based reranking. This section examines the first stage of DeGMatch and verifies that the relevance gate restricts gradient-based selection to a target-relevant candidate region without determining the final selected subset. Unless otherwise specified, the analyses use the AIME target with a 10K final selection budget. The subset-level diagnostics characterize how the gate changes the candidate region and selected data, while Section C.1 additionally evaluates downstream sensitivity to gate size.

C.1 Effect of Gate Size

The gate size controls how far gradient-based selection can search beyond the trajectories most similar to the target references. Table 23 varies the gate size while keeping the final selection budget fixed at B=10B=10K.

A smaller gate constrains selection to trajectories that are more semantically similar to the target references, while expanding the gate gives gradient matching access to longer and higher-NLL trajectories. When G=BG=B, the gate itself determines the final subset, reducing selection to semantic retrieval. At the other extreme, removing the gate increases the selected token volume from 68.9M to 115.8M and reduces AIME similarity from 0.531 to 0.493.

The default 3​B3B gate lies between these two extremes. It retains a target-relevant candidate region while leaving two-thirds of the gated examples available for student-specific reranking. These subset-level statistics alone do not establish a downstream-optimal gate size; we therefore evaluate downstream sensitivity separately below.

Downstream sensitivity to gate size.

The preceding diagnostics characterize how the relevance gate changes the candidate region and the resulting selected subset. We additionally evaluate whether these differences translate to downstream performance. Using a fixed 3K final selection budget, we vary the AIME relevance-gate size while keeping the gradient representation, scoring rule, and downstream training procedure unchanged. Table 24 reports the resulting downstream performance.

Performance remains similar across the finite gate sizes, with the 30K gate achieving the strongest average among the evaluated settings. In contrast, removing the relevance restriction and reranking over the full candidate pool reduces the average score to 33.90. These results suggest that the benefit of the relevance stage is not tied to a narrowly tuned gate size: a range of target-restricted candidate regions performs comparably, while eliminating the gate altogether is less effective.

C.2 Embedding Representation and Retrieval Aggregation

The round-robin construction in Section 3.2 is designed to prevent references with unusually dense neighborhoods from dominating the relevance gate. Table 25 compares the default construction with alternative embedding representations and aggregation rules, while fixing the gate size at 30K.

Round-robin retrieval provides substantially more balanced coverage across target references. Under the default construction, even the least-covered reference retains 893 of its 1,000 nearest candidates, whereas the minimum coverage falls to 96 under max-similarity aggregation and to 40 under mean-similarity aggregation. Notably, max-similarity aggregation achieves slightly higher overall AIME similarity than round-robin (0.522 vs. 0.519) despite this sharp reduction in worst-case coverage. This supports round-robin retrieval as a coverage-preserving rather than similarity-maximizing design, preventing the gate from concentrating around only a subset of reference neighborhoods.

The choice of embedding representation also matters. Replacing Qwen3-Embedding-8B with hidden states from the initial student yields a gate with a Jaccard similarity of 0.30 to the default gate and reduces both neighborhood coverage and AIME similarity. We therefore use a dedicated embedding model to identify the semantically relevant candidate region and reserve the student model for the subsequent gradient-based utility estimate.

C.3 Post-Hoc Proximity to Evaluation Problems

We additionally examine whether the target-reference gate identifies problems related to held-out evaluation instances. This analysis is strictly post hoc: evaluation problems are never used to construct the gate, compute gradients, or select training examples.

For each AIME24 or AIME25 problem, we retrieve its ten nearest problems from a given training set using the same Qwen3 problem embeddings and average their cosine similarities. Table 26 reports this nearest-neighbor proximity together with the average number of neighbors per evaluation problem whose cosine similarity exceeds 0.7.

The 30K relevance gate is substantially closer to AIME24/25 than Random or Length, providing additional evidence that the independently constructed reference set retrieves a candidate region related to the intended target capability. The final DeGMatch subset remains more target-proximal than Random and Length, but is less similar than the full relevance gate.

The lower proximity of the final DeGMatch subset relative to the full gate is consistent with the role of the second stage: after semantic retrieval defines a relevant candidate region, gradient matching is not constrained to choose the semantically nearest problems. Instead, it reranks the gate according to student-specific training utility. We emphasize that these evaluation-set similarities are used only for retrospective analysis and play no role in the selection procedure.

Appendix D Characteristics of Selected Reasoning Data

We examine the characteristics of the trajectories selected by DeGMatch and compare them with those produced by heuristic and target-aware alternatives. Unless otherwise specified, this section analyzes 10K mathematical trajectories selected for the AIME target.

D.1 Properties of the Selected Subset

Table 27 compares the resulting subsets in terms of trajectory length, student NLL, gradient norm, semantic similarity to the AIME references, and coarse problem composition. To summarize subject composition compactly, we report the combined fraction of examples labeled Number Theory or Combinatorics in the dataset metadata, together with the fraction carrying the olympiads source tag.

DeGMatch does not simply reproduce a single coarse selection heuristic. Its trajectories are substantially shorter than those selected by Length, with a median of 9.2K versus 13.9K tokens, while their student NLL is less extreme than MaxPPL. At the same time, DeGMatch has the highest semantic similarity to the AIME references among the compared 10K subsets.

The instance-level overlap tells a similar story. DeGMatch shares only 31% of its examples with Length, 30% with MaxPPL, 35% with RDS+, and 11% with Random. Its selected subset therefore cannot be characterized solely as choosing long trajectories, high-loss trajectories, or the examples most similar under a representation-level target metric.

Length-controlled comparison.

The descriptive statistics above show that DeGMatch differs substantially from explicit length-based selection, but trajectory length could still partially explain its downstream performance. We therefore construct a length-controlled random baseline from the same 30K AIME relevance gate used by the 3K DeGMatch analysis. After excluding the DeGMatch-selected examples, we partition the remaining candidates into 20 quantiles by complete training-sequence length and sample from each stratum to match the length distribution of the DeGMatch subset. Sampling uses seed 0 and does not use gradients.33 3 The longest stratum is short by 116 examples after excluding the DeGMatch subset; we fill this deficit from the adjacent shorter stratum. Table 28 reports the downstream comparison.

DeGMatch achieves a higher average score than the length-controlled random baseline (34.83 vs. 33.70), including improvements on AIME25 and AIME26. The two subsets have zero instance overlap while closely matching in both total token volume (36.1M vs. 35.3M) and median trajectory length (12,274 vs. 12,102 tokens). Because both subsets are drawn from the same relevance gate and have closely matched length distributions, the performance difference cannot be explained solely by semantic gating or trajectory length. This provides complementary evidence that gradient-based reranking captures information beyond these two factors.

D.2 Target-Specificity of the Selected Subsets

We next examine how strongly target-aware selectors respond to changes in the supplied target references. For each method, we independently select 10K trajectories for AIME, AMC, Gaokao, HMMT, and MATH500 and measure the pairwise Jaccard overlap among the resulting target-specific subsets.

Table 29 first reports the full pairwise overlap for DeGMatch. Competition-style targets share more selected data with each other than with MATH500 or Gaokao. AIME–HMMT overlap is 0.27 and AIME–AMC overlap is 0.21, whereas AIME overlaps with MATH500 and Gaokao by only 0.12 and 0.11. The target-specific subsets therefore share a common pool of potentially useful reasoning trajectories while still changing substantially with the supplied target capability.

Comparisons with existing target-aware selectors are provided in Appendix B.5. DeGMatch has a mean pairwise overlap of 0.15, compared with 0.253 at the relevance-gate level, showing that the gradient stage adds target differentiation beyond semantic retrieval alone. Importantly, we do not interpret lower overlap as intrinsically better: TAROT produces even lower cross-target overlap, yet does not outperform the strongest target-agnostic baselines in downstream evaluation. Rather, these diagnostics show that existing target-aware methods differ substantially in how strongly their selections respond to the supplied target references, and that DeGMatch produces target-dependent subsets without explicitly optimizing for low overlap.

D.3 How Deconfounding Changes Candidate Rankings

We finally examine which candidates undergo the largest rank changes after dominant-component removal. Table 30 compares trajectories that move from the raw-gradient top 1K to below rank 10K with trajectories that move from outside the raw top 10K into the DeGMatch top 1K.

The promoted examples are not simply shorter or lower-loss trajectories. In fact, candidates moving into the DeGMatch top 1K are longer and have higher median student NLL than those strongly demoted by deconfounding. This provides an additional indication that dominant-component removal does not act as a simple correction for trajectory length or difficulty.

The problem-type composition also changes: the promoted group contains more combinatorics and number-theory problems, whereas the demoted group contains more geometry and algebra problems. We treat this shift as descriptive rather than as evidence that any particular subject category is intrinsically more useful. The important observation is that removing dominant population structure substantially reorders candidates even when they occupy similar ranges of coarse trajectory characteristics.

D.4 Illustrative Target Matches

We provide qualitative examples of how deconfounded gradient matching relates target references to selected training trajectories. For a given target reference, ranks are computed among the 30K examples in its AIME relevance gate. To avoid trivial matches, we exclude candidate–reference pairs whose Qwen3 problem-embedding cosine similarity is at least 0.90. This filtering is used only for the qualitative analysis.

Table 31 presents two candidates selected for the same AIME reference, AIME 2020-II-9, a combinatorics problem involving arrangements subject to forbidden adjacencies. The first candidate is also semantically close to the reference, whereas the second is semantically more distant but uses a closely related reasoning procedure.

Example A is an intuitive match: both the reference and selected problem ask for arrangements under forbidden-adjacency constraints. Although it is the nearest candidate by semantic similarity, it ranks only 6,879th under raw-gradient cosine and rises to rank 1 after deconfounding. This example illustrates how dominant population-level gradient structure can down-rank even a semantically obvious target match under raw gradient similarity.

Example B illustrates a different behavior. Its surface form is substantially less similar to the reference, ranking 4,862th by problem-embedding similarity and 14,215th by raw-gradient cosine, but it rises to rank 13 after deconfounding. Inspection of the reasoning trajectories reveals a shared solution procedure: both define forbidden-adjacency events, merge adjacent objects into single blocks to count constrained arrangements, and use inclusion–exclusion to combine overlapping cases. The match is therefore consistent with DeGMatch prioritizing candidates with shared reasoning structure despite limited surface similarity.

These examples are intended only as qualitative illustrations. The aggregate analyses in Sections B.6 and D.3 provide quantitative evidence for the broader effect of deconfounding on target-conditioned rankings.

Appendix E Additional Experimental Results

E.1 Component-Validation Details

Table 32 summarizes the variants used in Section 6.1. All gradient-based variants select 3K examples from the same fixed 30K AIME relevance gate and differ only in the gradient transformation or scoring terms used within the gate. Relevance only selects directly from the semantic retrieval ranking, while Random samples from the full candidate pool. Raw-gradient direction uses directional target matching without gradient transformation; Centered direction additionally subtracts the candidate-population mean; and Deconfounded direction further removes the top 50 principal directions. Deconfounded magnitude uses the same transformed gradients but scores candidates only by target-subspace magnitude, whereas DeGMatch combines directional alignment and target-subspace magnitude multiplicatively.

Gate-controlled heuristic baselines.

The relevance gate itself may improve strong target-agnostic heuristics by restricting selection to a target-relevant candidate region. To separate this effect from the subsequent gradient-based reranking, we apply Length and MaxPPL directly within the same 30K AIME relevance gate used by DeGMatch. Table 33 reports the resulting 10K-example subsets.

Relevance gating improves both heuristics: Length increases from 58.73 to 59.11 average performance, while MaxPPL increases from 57.93 to 58.79. However, DeGMatch remains stronger at 60.73 while using fewer training tokens. Thus, the performance of DeGMatch is not explained by simply applying a strong length- or difficulty-based heuristic within the relevance gate.

Sensitivity to magnitude scaling.

We further examine the role of target-subspace magnitude in the DeGMatch score. Prior work has shown that sequence length can systematically affect gradient-based influence scores, motivating gradient normalization to mitigate length-dependent selection bias (Wang et al., 2025). We therefore test both how strongly magnitude should enter the score and whether its contribution can be explained primarily by trajectory length.

We first vary the strength of the magnitude term using di​miγd_{i}m_{i}^{\gamma} with γ∈{0,12,1,2}\gamma\in\{0,\frac{1}{2},1,2\}, where γ=0\gamma=0 corresponds to directional matching alone and γ=1\gamma=1 is the default DeGMatch score. In our setting, mim_{i} is strongly positively correlated with trajectory length (Spearman ρ=0.85\rho=0.85), so we additionally consider two length-adjusted variants. The first uses di​mi/Tid_{i}m_{i}/\sqrt{T_{i}}, where TiT_{i} is the number of tokens in the complete training sequence. For the second, we fit

log⁡mi=α^+β^​log⁡Ti+ϵi\log m_{i}=\hat{\alpha}+\hat{\beta}\log T_{i}+\epsilon_{i}

by ordinary least squares over all 30K candidates in the AIME relevance gate and define

mires=log⁡mi−(α^+β^​log⁡Ti).m_{i}^{\mathrm{res}}=\log m_{i}-(\hat{\alpha}+\hat{\beta}\log T_{i}).

We obtain β^=0.54\hat{\beta}=0.54. The resulting score di​exp⁡(mires)d_{i}\exp(m_{i}^{\mathrm{res}}) is rank-equivalent, up to a positive constant, to di​mi/Tiβ^d_{i}m_{i}/T_{i}^{\hat{\beta}} and reduces the Spearman correlation with trajectory length from 0.850.85 to 0.080.08.

Table 34 reports the downstream results. The default di​mid_{i}m_{i} achieves the strongest average performance, while the squared-magnitude and length-residualized variants remain close. Notably, removing most of the empirical association between magnitude and trajectory length leaves performance nearly unchanged, suggesting that the benefit of target-subspace magnitude is not explained solely by selecting longer trajectories. Overall, the results support the simple multiplicative score while indicating that its effectiveness is not narrowly tied to either a particular magnitude exponent or trajectory length.

E.2 Per-Target Selection Statistics

Because reasoning trajectories vary substantially in length, equal example budgets can correspond to very different amounts of training supervision. Table 35 reports the number of training tokens in each 10K-example mathematical subset. Counts are measured with the student-model tokenizer over the complete training sequence and correspond to a single training epoch. Select2Reason is omitted because we evaluate its released checkpoint rather than a budget-matched subset selected under our pipeline.

Despite using the same 10K-example budget, the target-agnostic subsets vary substantially in training-token volume, from 34.9M tokens for RSR to 142.3M for Length, a 4.1×\times difference. In particular, RSR contains substantially fewer training tokens than Random (34.9M vs. 60.3M), illustrating that matching the number of selected examples does not imply a matched amount of training supervision. Target-aware methods also vary across target capabilities: for example, RDS+ ranges from 56.6M tokens for MATH500 to 110.0M for HMMT, while DeGMatch ranges from 69.7M to 102.0M. These statistics motivate reporting both example and token budgets when comparing reasoning-data selection methods.
